subjects.introduction: A soul can become something other than it was. Bahá’u’lláh places the beginning of that change not in private resolve but in a Divine Springtime: the same sun, the same rain, and yet one tree turns green while its neighbour withers. The difference lies in what a heart has made of itself, a mirror polished or left to rust, a wick that catches at a touch where stone lies cold in the fire for a thousand years. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes the result in the plainest terms: the same person in form, yet in character another, the quick temper turned to calm and pride to humility. The road there passes through winter, since the soil that is ploughed yields most and pure gold does not fear the fire. To follow it farther is to ask what the divine elixir does to the copper of a life, what it means to be born a second time out of the world of nature, and how the Holy Spirit works like fire on iron, turning its blackness to red and its coldness to heat.

order.why: These readings begin with the source of transformation. In the Kitáb-i-Íqán Bahá’u’lláh asks whether the object of every Revelation is not to effect a transformation in the whole character of mankind, both outwardly and inwardly. He announces that the Divine Springtime is come, and observes how many trees of human souls have become fresh and verdant in this springtide while others in the same season have withered. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that Bahá’u’lláh has renewed that springtime, with the same fragrances, the same heat of the Sun and the same cloud, and that when the Manifestation casts His splendour on hearts a spiritual springtime is ushered in. Reported talks call the Teachings the breaths of the Holy Spirit that create men anew. Why do the Writings place the beginning of transformation in the coming of a Manifestation rather than in individual effort? What does the image of spring suggest about how such change happens?
shortened: And yet, is not the object of every Revelation to effect a transformation in the whole character of mankind, a transformation that shall manifest itself, both outwardly and inwardly, that shall affect both its inner life and external conditions? For if the character of mankind be not changed, the futility of God's universal Manifestation would be apparent.

A new springtime arrived, and a vivifying breeze wafted; the clouds rained down, and that Day-Star of loving-kindness shone resplendent. These readings take up the Divine Elixir. Bahá’u’lláh speaks of His most exalted Word, ordained as the Divine Elixir through whose potency the crude metal of human life has been transmuted into purest gold, and of a few who have been endued with that Elixir and with the infallible remedy for the ills of men. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to find the Alchemy of Truth and cast it upon the copper and iron of men’s souls, and says the Prophets appear so that the lump of coal may become a diamond. Through divine power the mosquito becomes an eagle, the shell a pearl and dust the philosopher’s stone. Beside the elixir stands the remedy: no disease is greater than heedlessness and hate, and no remedy more potent than the Word of God. What does the language of alchemy say that the language of improvement cannot? Why must patients first be made aware of their illness?
shortened: O handmaiden of God! Illnesses are of two kinds: spiritual and physical. Physical illnesses are cured through medicines, essences of herbs and drugs. But illnesses that result from psychic conditions are treated through the power of the human spirit. However, the power of the divine spirit rules over both physical and psychic conditions. Therefore when the human spirit becomes confirmed by the Holy Spirit's reinforcements, it can have its effects at every level in the world of existence.

These readings describe awakening and the quickening of the dead. Bahá’u’lláh prays, I lay asleep on the bed of self when lo, Thou didst waken me with the divine accents of Thy voice, and says that He found man asleep and awakened him, distant and drew him near, mute and caused him to speak. By graves, He explains, is meant heedlessness of self and passion, a death more severe than physical death; and he who walks and speaks may be counted among the dead. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls Christ’s words, Let the dead bury the dead, describes souls dead in the graves of desire raised by the trumpet blast of the Abhá Kingdom, and a reported talk notes that some wake at a touch while others need the noise of a cannon. Prayers ask, I am earthly; make me heavenly. What distinguishes outward life from the life these passages mean? What might it take to wake a heavy sleeper?
shortened: The first utterance of Him Who is the All-Wise is this: O children of dust! Turn your faces from the darkness of estrangement to the effulgent light of the daystar of unity. This is that which above all else will benefit the peoples of the earth.

order.why: These readings turn to the second birth. Reported talks recall Christ’s saying, Ye must be born again, and explain that as a child is born from the womb of its mother into this world, so a soul is born out of the world of nature into the world of the spirit through divine education. The embryo is alive but counted as dead until it is born, and the pain of birth is a gift. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of baptism with the water of life, the fire of the love of God and the Holy Spirit, and defines eternal life as receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, as a flower receives the breezes of spring. Bahá’u’lláh writes that the life mentioned in the Books of the Prophets is the life of knowledge. You must be newly created, one talk says; your very being must be transformed. What does the analogy of birth teach about the powers a soul receives before it can use them? Can a second birth happen gradually?
shortened: That life, however, which is mentioned in the Books of the Prophets and the Chosen Ones of God is the life of knowledge; that is to say, the servant's recognition of the sign of the splendours wherewith He Who is the Source of all splendour hath Himself invested him, and his certitude of attaining unto the presence of God through the Manifestations of His Cause. This is that blessed and everlasting life that perisheth not: whosoever is quickened thereby shall never die, but will endure as long as His Lord and Creator will endure.

order.why: These readings use the image of iron in the fire. Reported talks compare human nature to iron, black, cold and solid, and the grace of the Holy Spirit to fire that turns its blackness to redness and its coldness to heat, and explain sacrifice as a reality giving up its own characteristics, as the seed gives itself up so that the plant may appear. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that one who loses his I-hood sees with the eye of God, and that until the old garment is torn the new robe cannot be donned. Bahá’u’lláh calls true sacrifice the submerging of one’s will in the Will of God, says that without the fire of separation the Kawthar of nearness will not flow, and compares man to a sword whose quality stays unknown while it is sheathed in the scabbard of self. What does the iron give up, and what does it keep? How do these passages distinguish detachment from loss?
shortened: Blessed is the man who hath detached himself from all else but Me, hath soared in the atmosphere of My love, hath gained admittance into My Kingdom, gazed upon My realms of glory, quaffed the living waters of My bounty, hath drunk his fill from the heavenly river of My loving providence, acquainted himself with My Cause, apprehended that which I concealed within the treasury of My Words, and hath shone forth from the horizon of divine knowledge engaged in My praise and glorification.

These readings consider capacity and the purified heart. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that however mighty the outpouring of grace, souls must become receptive and worthy; a reported talk adds that the mirror must be cleared of rust before the sun is reflected, as one prepares the apartment before inviting the guest. Stone and clay may lie in fire a thousand years without effect while the wick of a lamp blazes at a touch, and a black stone cannot become a ruby. Reported talks ask that the soil of hearts be freed of weeds and thorns, and say that capacity grows through detachment from the world and attraction to God. Bahá’u’lláh writes that all He has endured has one purpose, that hearts may be sanctified from selfish inclinations, and that the fast decreases the carnal and increases the spiritual; the Báb asks that the earth of souls be purified. Is capacity given or acquired? What in these passages prepares a heart to receive?

These readings describe transformation as growth through stages. Bahá’u’lláh counsels, In every breath be other than thy former self, and with every step advance beyond thy previous step, and describes seas of search, love and detachment. The Báb calls the whole Law a path for the servant to journey toward his Lord and traces how knowledge leads to fear, fear to flight and flight to salvation. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes progress in station from progress in perfections and hopes that a drop may expand day by day into a boundless ocean. Reported talks say that the soul evolves only nearer to God, liken the spirit to a muscle strengthened by exercise, advise comparing today with yesterday each morning, and warn that stagnation is the beginning of retrogression. At the gate of the garden some look in and only a few penetrate. What makes spiritual progress measurable, if anything? Why is standing still described as falling back?
shortened: That divine world is manifestly a world of lights; therefore, man has need of illumination here. That is a world of love; the love of God is essential. It is a world of perfections; virtues, or perfections, must be acquired. That world is vivified by the breaths of the Holy Spirit; in this world we must seek them. That is the Kingdom of everlasting life; it must be attained during this vanishing existence.

These readings look for transformation in character and conduct. Bahá’u’lláh hopes that each may adorn himself with pure and holy deeds, calls striving with one’s own self the greater striving, and asks that once the heart is purified the believer act on the Tablets so that the outward temple too becomes pure. Reported talks describe a person who remains the same in form but in character has become another, observe that a moral teacher may labour to remove one fault while the dawning of faith changes a person wholly, ask that quick temper be changed into calmness and pride into humility, insist on complete regeneration rather than a change of name, and say of one transformed believer that she is the proof of Bahá’u’lláh. Narratives tell of Gregory, of Mírzá ‘Alí-Akbar re-created within minutes, and of Abu Dharr and Bilal. How can others recognize a changed life? Which qualities in these accounts change first?
shortened: I beseech God that He may graciously enable every one of you to adorn himself, in this blessed Day, with the ornament of pure and holy deeds.

order.why: These readings treat transformation as nurture and education. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes to children as saplings grown in the garden of the love of God and prays that tender plants become verdant through the clouds of mercy. He hopes that education will transform earthly children into heavenly youths, and that children fostered in the shell of education will grow like pearls of divine bounty. He asks the friends to train the souls of men until frenzied beasts change to gazelles and wolves to lambs. Reported talks say that children are like green branches that can be trained while still supple, and that without an educator humanity cannot progress in spiritual affairs and divine morals; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the first work is attraction and enkindlement, after which comes the training of the soul. Why do these passages give the educator so large a part? What is the difference between training and transformation?
shortened: His purpose is this, that we, all of us, should strive with our whole hearts to offer ourselves up, guide others to His path, and train the souls of men--until these frenzied beasts change to gazelles in the meadows of oneness, and these wolves to lambs of God, and these brutish creatures to angelic hosts; till the fires of hatred are quenched, and the flame coming out of the sheltered vale of the Holy Shrine doth shed its splendors; till the foul odor of the tyrant's dunghill is blown away, and yieldeth to the pure, sweet scents that stream from the rosebeds of faith and trust.

The readings close with prayers for transformation. Bahá’u’lláh calls on God by the Name through which He turns restlessness into tranquillity, fear into confidence, weakness into strength and abasement into glory, and asks for what will purify the soul of all that is not of Him and detach it from all else. He asks to quaff the living waters that free those who drink from attachment and enable them to soar in the atmosphere of His nearness. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays, Bestow upon me a pure heart, like unto a pearl, and asks that God deliver the soul from darkness and make it a brilliant light. A prayer of the Báb recalls how, on reaching maturity, He was educated through the subtle operations of God’s grace. Which requests in these prayers echo the images of the earlier sections? What part do the prayers give to God and what part to the one who prays?
shortened: Through the spirit of power confirm Thou me in Thy Cause, O my Best-Beloved, and by the light of Thy glory reveal unto me Thy path, O Thou the Goal of my desire!

In these authorized words from a talk in Paris ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes that His hearers may give sight to the spiritually blind, hearing to the spiritually deaf and life to those who are dead in sin, and that they may help those sunk in materiality to realize their divine sonship. The supplied quotation stops before the clause on the world becoming the Kingdom of God; the approximate status is preserved. Compare it with the readings on awakening and on transforming others. What birthright is meant here?

The second sentence, the cry of the Furthermost Mosque for having been quickened by the breeze of God’s nearness after being slain by separation, is a different rendering of the cry the authorized text gives to Jerusalem, so the approximate status is preserved. Read it with the readings on quickening. What does it mean for a holy place to be quickened?

This supplied provisional rendering of a Tablet of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that God rejects distinctions of race and border, that all the divine teachings aim at improving human character, and that only the power of the Holy Spirit can transform man, bestowing the second birth and baptizing him with the fire of the love of God, which is love for all created things. The catalogue renders the same paragraphs differently, and neither rendering is authorized; the approximate status is preserved. Why does this passage tie the second birth to love for all creation?
shortened: All the divine teachings can be summarized as this: that these thoughts singling out advantages to one group may be banished from our midst, that human character may be improved, that equality and fellowship may be established amongst all mankind, until every individual is ready to sacrifice himself for the sake of his fellowman.

The outpourings of the Holy Spirit are such that they can transform man, imbuing him with all the virtues, bestowing upon him the second birth, baptizing him with the fire of the love of God, which is love for all created things, and quickening him with the water of eternal life, and the Holy Spirit itself.

questions: The readings describe transformation through many images: spring, alchemy, birth, waking, iron in the fire. Choose two of these images and compare them. What does each reveal about the change that the other does not?

Some passages say the change can happen in an instant, more swiftly than the twinkling of an eye; others describe slow growth through stages, day by day. How can both be true, and what do the narratives in the section on character suggest?

Many readings insist that grace is mighty but souls must become receptive and worthy. What part do the readings give to divine power and what part to human effort? Look at the wick and the stone, the polished mirror, and the counsel to compare today with yesterday.

Why do so many passages connect transformation with tests and suffering? Consider the soil that is ploughed, gold in the fire and winter before spring, and ask what the readings say a person should do during a test.

The Kitáb-i-Íqán says that a Revelation should transform the character of mankind both outwardly and inwardly. What signs of inward change do the readings describe, and how do they say it should appear in conduct, in families and in society?
Several prayers ask God to make the one who prays heavenly, pure or detached. How might praying in this way take part in the process the other readings describe?
